items.prompt: Why is depth called expensive?
choices: Each hour spent going deep is unavailable for other topics
Deep study always produces worse results
Depth cannot be measured in hours at all
items.explanation: Hours are a fixed pool, so depth on one topic is paid for with every other topic.

items.prompt: Marco split 20 hours evenly across 6 topics. Roughly how many hours did each get?
choices: About 2 hours
About 5 hours
About 3.3 hours
items.explanation: 20 divided by 6 is about 3.3.

items.prompt: How many hours did Sofia put into her two focus topics together?
choices: 10 hours
20 hours
15 hours
items.explanation: 15 of her 20 hours went to visa paperwork and the bank account; the other 5 were shared by four topics.

items.prompt: What did Marco's even split ignore?
choices: That 20 hours is simply too little time to study with
That some topics matter far more
That six topics is too long a list to write down well
items.explanation: An even split gives slang the same attention as visa paperwork.

items.prompt: Which topic caused Marco's weeks of trouble?
choices: Tipping customs, which he overstudied for weeks
Visa and bank paperwork, thinly covered
Transit, which he skipped
items.explanation: His paperwork topics got the same hours as low-stakes ones.

items.prompt: Which statement about Sofia and Marco is true?

Sofia studied more total hours than Marco did

items.explanation: Total hours and list were identical; only the split differed.

It avoids deciding anything at all, which is safe

items.explanation: Spreading evenly is still an allocation, just an unexamined one.

items.prompt: How did Sofia learn tipping customs?

From a phrasebook
Free, from a coworker on day two
items.explanation: Cheap-to-learn topics can be picked up when needed at almost no cost.

items.prompt: Two learners each have 12 hours for four topics. One gives 3 hours to each topic. The other gives 5 hours to each of the two most failure-prone topics and 1 hour to each of the others. What does this comparison show?
choices: Equal totals can give unequal outcomes, because the split decides what is covered
The even split is safer because each topic gets at least three hours
The focused split only wins if the learner studies more than 12 hours
Both splits are equivalent because the total number of hours is identical
items.explanation: 5 + 5 + 1 + 1 = 12, the same total as 4 x 3. The difference is which topics are prepared when the stakes arrive.
items.reference:
Same 20 hours, different splits
📊 Marco: 6 topics x 3.3 hours
🎯 Sofia: 2 topics x 7.5 hours, 4 topics x 1.25 hours
⚖️ Both columns add up to 20
Why: depth is a fixed budget, so every hour spent deep on one topic is gone for the others.
items.learnMore:
Depth is a fixed budget

Hours spent going deep on one topic cannot be spent again. An even split is therefore a choice: it says every topic matters equally.

Common mistake

Treating an even split as the neutral, risk-free option.
items.reflection: Think of something you recently spread your time across evenly. Which part deserved far more of it?

items.prompt: A friend says: 'I'll spread my time evenly so nothing catches me off guard.' What assumption is hiding in that plan?
choices: That studying quickly always beats studying slowly in every situation
That skimming a topic is always worse than ignoring it entirely
That the total number of hours can be raised later at no cost at all
That every topic is equally likely and equally risky
items.explanation: An even split only makes sense if the topics are interchangeable in stakes. Visa paperwork and slang are not.

Skipping a topic forever

Studying ahead of any need
Learning only from a coworker who offers help

Study with no concrete need
Looking a topic up when it comes up

The price of the study materials
How long ago you first heard about the topic
items.explanation: It measures time, difficulty or deadlines, not money for books.

items.prompt: What makes just-in-time safe for a topic?
choices: A low cost to learn it later
A high chance you will forget it
A long list of other topics
items.explanation: If learning at the moment of need is cheap, waiting costs little.

Is required by law
Makes many other things easier to learn
items.explanation: Its value comes from what it unlocks.

items.prompt: Which three things does the triage heuristic weigh?

Price, speed, and how much you enjoy it all

A coworker could teach it cheaply later

items.explanation: Low cost to learn later makes waiting safe.

items.prompt: A topic has a filing deadline two weeks into your first month, and learning it then would be rushed and error-prone. Which approach fits?
choices: Learn it just-in-time, because the need is certain to arrive
Learn it deeply now, because learning later is costly
Skip it, because deadlines can usually be extended
Study it just in case, because it might matter someday
items.explanation: Certain need does not make waiting safe. The narrow window makes later learning expensive, which is the signal for depth now.
items.reference:
Two ways to time your learning
⏱️ Just-in-time: shallow now, proper study when the need arrives
🎒 Just-in-case: study now because it might matter
🔑 Cost to learn later decides which is safe
Why: just-in-time is safe only when picking the topic up later is cheap.
items.learnMore:
Just-in-time vs. just-in-case

Waiting is safe when learning later is quick and has no deadline. Studying early pays mainly when a topic is foundational or has a narrow window.

Common mistake

Treating just-in-time as always safe, even for topics with deadlines.

items.prompt: Learning a city's bus routes is very likely to matter, but a map app explains them in minutes. Which zone is this?
choices: Likely and costly later, so deep now
Unlikely and cheap later, so skip
Unlikely and costly later, so cheap skim
Likely and cheap later, so just-in-time

items.reference:
Four zones
🎯 Likely + costly later: deep now
⏱️ Likely + cheap later: just-in-time
🛡️ Unlikely + costly later: cheap skim
🗑️ Unlikely + cheap later: skip
Why: likelihood and cost-to-learn-later are independent, so crossing them gives four different treatments.
items.learnMore:
Two questions, four zones

Likelihood tells you whether a topic will come up. Cost to learn later tells you whether waiting is safe. Only the combination says how much study it earns.

Common mistake

Using one question alone: studying every likely topic, or skipping every unlikely one.

items.prompt: With 30 hours, 75% reserved, and 3 flagged topics, how many hours does each flagged topic get?
choices: 7.5 hours
10 hours
5 hours
22.5 hours
items.explanation: 30 x 0.75 = 22.5, divided by 3 = 7.5. The 22.5 figure is the total reserved, not the per-topic share.
items.reference:
20 hours, 75% reserved (15 hours)
1 flagged topic: 15 hours each
2 flagged topics: 7.5 hours each
3 flagged topics: 5 hours each
6 flagged topics: 2.5 hours each
Why: the reserved hours are divided among every flagged topic, so each added priority thins the rest.
items.learnMore:
The budget is shared

Hours per flagged topic equal the reserved hours divided by the number of flagged topics. Adding a priority never adds hours.

Common mistake

Flagging everything as important, which recreates an even split.

items.learnMore:
Method versus inputs

A triage is only as good as its estimates. Reasoning by analogy to a low-stakes topic is a guess; a five-minute check for deadlines turns it into an input you can trust.

Common mistake

Blaming the method, or dropping it, after one bad outcome.
items.reflection: Think of a past decision that went badly. Was the reasoning flawed, or one of its inputs?

Method versus inputs

A triage is only as good as its estimates. Reasoning by analogy to a low-stakes topic is a guess; a five-minute check for deadlines turns it into an input you can trust.

Common mistake

Blaming the method, or dropping it, after one bad outcome.
items.reflection: Think of a past decision that went badly. Was the reasoning flawed, or one of its inputs?

items.prompt: Three days remain before the window closes. What is the most efficient move?
choices: Research the whole system from scratch before filing
Wait for the window to pass and then reapply later
Ask a person who has done it, then file today
Study other topics first to lower the stress level
items.explanation: Time is the scarce input; a person who knows the process is faster than self-study.
items.reference:
Sofia's health insurance miss (assumed rules)
🧮 Scored: cheap to learn later
📅 Actual: 10-day window from the day residency clears
⏳ Found out on day 17, 3 days left
🤝 Fixed with help from her employer's HR contact
Why: a sound process can still fail when an input is a guess, so verify the inputs on high-consequence items.

items.prompt: Which question, asked of every high-consequence item, would have exposed the miss?
choices: Is this topic more fun than the others?
Is a deadline attached to this?
How many hours did others spend on it?
Could anyone at all skip this topic?
items.explanation: A deadline check is the cheap verification that turns an analogy into an input.

items.prompt: When did local tax filing move to deep now?
choices: A tax form was due within a month
She finished the visa paperwork and moved on
She arrived and settled into her flat
items.explanation: New information changed the input.

items.prompt: Re-triage means...
choices: Starting over from zero
Skipping every topic until the end
Re-scoring on new information
items.explanation: Same method, updated inputs.

items.prompt: Was skipping tax filing on day one a mistake?
choices: Yes, she should have known everything beforehand
Only partly wrong
No, it was reasonable then
items.explanation: The score was right for the facts available.

items.prompt: What happened to transit on re-triage?
choices: It moved to deep now once she arrived
Score confirmed unchanged
It was dropped
items.explanation: It needed almost no study.

items.prompt: With only 2 hours, how many deep-now topics fit?
choices: Five
About one
Nine
items.explanation: Two hours leaves room for one topic, maybe part of one.

items.prompt: Which topic gets the 2 hours?
choices: Visa paperwork
Slang
Tipping customs
items.explanation: Its failure is the hardest to undo.

items.prompt: A smaller budget shrinks...
choices: Skim tier too, not only deep
Only the deep tier, nothing else
Nothing, since skims are free
items.explanation: Skim time is drawn from the same scarce hours.

items.prompt: Updating a triage score is...
choices: A sign of failure, so avoid it
Allowed once only
Normal and costs nothing
items.explanation: It is a habit, not an admission of error.

items.prompt: On day one tax filing was 'not due for months'. In week two her employer needs a form within a month. What is the best reading?
choices: The original reasoning was flawed and should be blamed
The input changed, so the score changes; the original call was reasonable
The new fact should be ignored to stay consistent
Every other topic should now be moved to deep now
items.explanation: The correction came from new information, not from an error in reasoning.
items.reference:
Triage is revisited, not fixed
📥 New fact: employer needs a tax form within a month
🔁 Tax filing moves from skip to deep now
✅ Transit score confirmed unchanged
📉 With 2 hours, only one topic fits deep
Why: scores rest on what is known at the time, so they should update when better information arrives.
items.learnMore:
Re-triage and shrinking budgets

When new facts replace guesses, re-score without guilt. When the budget shrinks, the deep tier narrows and the skim tier shrinks with it.

Common mistake

Defending the original score because changing it feels like admitting an error.
items.reflection: Which plan of yours is still running on day-one assumptions that you could re-score today?

items.prompt: The budget drops from 20 hours to 2 hours with the same list. Which statement is true?
choices: Same questions, but the skim tier shrinks too
The questions change, because skims no longer matter at all
Only the deep tier needs to shrink, the rest stays put
Every topic now gets an equal share of about 0.2 hours
items.explanation: Skim time comes from the same scarce pool, so fewer topics earn even a skim.

items.prompt: Which situation calls for a re-triage rather than keeping the plan?
choices: You feel anxious about a topic you decided to skip
A friend would have ranked the topics differently
A full week has passed and nothing at all new was learned
A coworker names a deadline you had scored as absent
items.explanation: Re-triage is triggered by new facts, not by feelings or others' preferences.
